items.followUp: Name two vitamins that function as co-enzymes.

rubric.why: Identifies the vitamin group that commonly acts as co-enzymes.
rubric.description: Names the B-complex vitamins as co-enzymes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying B-complex vitamins.

rubric.why: Gives examples of vitamins that act as co-enzymes.
rubric.description: Names examples such as vitamins B1, B2 or B3.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving two correct examples, or an equivalent specific pair.

modelAnswer: Examples include vitamins B1 (thiamine), B2 (riboflavin) and B3 (niacin).

items.followUp: Where is the electron transport chain located, and what is its main role in respiration?

rubric.why: Identifies where the electron transport chain is located.
rubric.description: States that the chain is in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct location.

rubric.why: Describes electron transfer and its role in ATP production.
rubric.description: Explains that electrons pass along carriers and the released energy is used to make ATP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking electron transfer with ATP production.

modelAnswer: The electron transport chain is a series of electron carriers in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Electrons from NADH and FADH₂ pass along the carriers, releasing energy used to produce ATP; oxygen is the final electron acceptor.

items.followUp: Write the word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining condition of anaerobic respiration.
rubric.description: States that respiration occurs without oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: Names the products of anaerobic respiration.
rubric.description: Gives ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast, or lactic acid in muscles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correct products in either yeast or muscle cells.

modelAnswer: Anaerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose to release energy without oxygen.
In yeast, glucose is converted into ethanol and carbon dioxide; in muscle cells, it forms lactic acid.

items.followUp: State where the Krebs cycle occurs and name two products formed during it.

rubric.why: Describes the Krebs cycle as a cyclic sequence of reactions.
rubric.description: Defines it as a cycle or series of reactions in respiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as a cyclic series of reactions.

rubric.why: Gives its location or identifies products formed in the cycle.
rubric.description: States that it occurs in the mitochondrial matrix and/or names products such as carbon dioxide, NADH, FADH₂ or ATP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct location or at least two correct products.

modelAnswer: The Krebs cycle is a cyclic series of reactions in which acetyl-CoA is broken down during cellular respiration.
It occurs in the mitochondrial matrix and produces carbon dioxide, ATP, NADH and FADH₂.

items.followUp: Define nutrition and state one reason organisms need nutrients.

rubric.why: States that nutrition involves obtaining or taking in food.
rubric.description: Defines nutrition as the process of obtaining or taking in food.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the food-intake part of the definition.

rubric.why: Includes the use of food or its purpose in the organism.
rubric.description: States that food is utilized for energy, growth, repair or maintenance.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining food use or a valid purpose.

modelAnswer: Nutrition is the process by which organisms obtain food and utilize it.
Food provides energy and materials needed for growth, repair and maintenance of the body.

items.followUp: Give two plant sources and two animal sources of proteins.

rubric.why: Identifies dietary plant sources of protein.
rubric.description: Gives one or more plant sources, such as pulses, beans, peas or nuts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correct plant sources.

rubric.why: Identifies dietary animal sources of protein.
rubric.description: Gives one or more animal sources, such as meat, fish, eggs or milk.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correct animal sources.

modelAnswer: Plant sources of proteins include pulses, beans, peas and nuts.
Animal sources of proteins include meat, fish, eggs and milk.

items.followUp: Name the two vascular tissues in plants and state what each transports.

rubric.why: States the transport role of xylem.
rubric.description: Explains that xylem transports water and mineral salts, mainly from roots to other parts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming xylem and its transported substances.

rubric.why: States the transport role of phloem.
rubric.description: Explains that phloem transports prepared food through the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming phloem and its transported material.

modelAnswer: The vascular system transports materials throughout the plant.
Xylem carries water and mineral salts from the roots, while phloem carries prepared food from the leaves to other parts.

items.followUp: Explain how transpiration helps water move from roots to leaves.

rubric.why: Connects transpiration with the force or pull it generates.
rubric.description: States that loss of water by transpiration creates a pulling force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking transpiration with the pull.

rubric.why: Describes the upward movement of water through the plant.
rubric.description: States that the pull draws water upward through xylem from roots toward leaves.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the direction and pathway of water movement.

modelAnswer: Transpirational pull is the pulling force produced when water evaporates from the leaves during transpiration.
It draws water upward through the xylem from the roots to the leaves.
